meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Your Bald Head Feels as Smooth as My Wife's Cheek'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Franklin P. Adams. The bald-head joke was an anonymous barber-shop gag in print by 1924; a 1934 joke book cast Adams as the heckler, not the wit.

answer.label: Not Franklin P. Adams — an anonymous barber-shop joke
answer.authorDates: American folk joke · in print by July 1924
answer.sourceLine: The comparison began as an anonymous barber-shop joke. It was printed in July 1924 as “your head feels just like my wife’s cheek,” and the earliest named person is S. H. Hale, who told it about a barber who worked for him. Adams’s name was attached only in a privately printed 1934 joke book. There he says a cruder version as the heckler, and Marc Connelly gets the comeback (Quote Investigator ↗).

source.heading: The earliest printed version

docMeta.dd: S. H. Hale, about a barber who had worked for him

source.excerpt: S. H. Hale tells this one on a fresh young barber he had working for him several years ago. This particular barber thought he would kid a bald-headed man. “Don’t you know,” he said, rubbing the bald spot, “your head feels just like my wife’s cheek”. The customer reached up and stroked his head for a moment and then said: “By golly it does, doesn’t it.”
trail: July 1924: the Roswell Daily Record prints S. H. Hale’s story of a barber who tells a bald customer “your head feels just like my wife’s cheek.” It is the earliest version Quote Investigator found ↗.

1934: the privately printed Anecdota Americana: Second Series has Franklin P. Adams put his hand on Mark [sic] Connelly’s head and make a cruder comparison. Connelly answers, “By God, Frank, so it does” (Quote Investigator ↗).
1968: Stewart Alsop’s The Center gives the comeback to Nicholas Longworth. Jane Grant’s memoir, also from 1968, gives it to Connelly at Tony’s (Quote Investigator ↗).

2015: on the American Dialect Society list, Garson O’Toole notes that the standard reference books’ earliest citations were from 1975 and 1976. He then announces the new entry, whose citations begin in 1924 (ADS-L ↗).
source.excerptNote: Text as transcribed by Quote Investigator. The neat wording “Your bald head feels as smooth as my wife’s cheek” is the title of Quote Investigator’s article, not a line from any period source.

author.name: Anonymous
author.heading: Who made the joke
author.metaLine: American folk joke · in print by 1924
author.bio: No author is known. The earliest printed version Quote Investigator found, in the Roswell Daily Record of July 12, 1924, gives the line to a “fresh young barber” teasing a bald customer, in a story told by S. H. Hale. Over the following decades the joke was retold about Algonquin Round Table wits, including Marc Connelly and Franklin P. Adams, and about House Speaker Nicholas Longworth.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why
misattribution.intro: This joke has been told about several bald men and their hecklers. Franklin P. Adams appears in it only as the heckler in one bawdy 1934 retelling. Quote Investigator found no version in which Adams delivers the punchline.

items.why: His name appears only in the privately printed Anecdota Americana: Second Series (1934). There he is the man who rubs Connelly’s head and makes the crude comparison. He is the butt of the joke, not its wit, and that is ten years after the barber-shop version was in print (Quote Investigator ↗).

Quote Investigator believes Connelly probably did deliver the punchline (“so it does”) at some point, perhaps re-enacting an existing joke. It also allows that the story may simply have been pinned on a witty bald man. Either way, the line about the wife belongs to the heckler, not to Connelly (Quote Investigator ↗).
He was first linked to the story in Stewart Alsop’s 1968 book, decades after his death in 1931. The barber-shop version had been printed before he became Speaker (Quote Investigator ↗).
The 1924 newspaper item credits Hale with telling the story about a barber who worked for him. Neither man is named as the author of the joke (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The line began as an anonymous barber-shop joke, printed in July 1924 as “your head feels just like my wife’s cheek.” Franklin P. Adams was written into a cruder 1934 version as the heckler (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why the wording keeps changing
lead: Quote Investigator calls the early evidence fragmentary and probably cleaned up. Newspapers in the 1920s printed “my wife’s cheek,” a double meaning a family paper could get away with. Papers in the 1950s used “my wife’s leg,” and later books printed “bottom,” “behind” and “backside.” In the printed record Quote Investigator found, the cruder word first appears in a privately printed 1934 collection.

The Algonquin Round Table versions attach the story to famous names. Adams and Connelly were both charter members of the group, which lunched at the Algonquin Hotel from 1919 until roughly 1929, according to Wikipedia ↗. Even in those versions, the wit is the bald man who answers, not the man who makes the comparison.
context.pull: By golly it does, doesn’t it.
